definitions.definition: A way to describe how something shrinks quickly at first, then slows down as it gets smaller.
definitions.example: Like a bouncing ball that bounces high at first, then lower and lower until it barely moves.

definitions.definition: The lowest value a decreasing number can reach, like a bottom limit it can't go below.
definitions.example: A car's gas gauge can't go below 'empty'—that's the floor.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system; things tend to get more messy over time.
definitions.example: Your bedroom gets messier on its own, but it takes work to clean it up.

definitions.definition: When something builds on itself, like interest on money or problems that get worse because each step adds to the last.
definitions.example: If you skip one homework assignment, it's easy to skip another, and soon you're way behind.

definitions.definition: When a system loses its organized, connected state and becomes more random or separate.
definitions.example: A choir singing in harmony slowly falling out of tune with each other.

definitions.definition: In Christian thought, the divine reason or order that God used to create and sustain the universe; often identified with Jesus Christ.
definitions.example: Like the blueprint or master plan that keeps everything running smoothly.

definitions.definition: The idea that disorder and brokenness build up from one generation to the next, like a family curse of bad habits.
definitions.example: If your grandparents had poor health, your parents might have worse health, and you might have even more problems.

definitions.definition: A theoretical field in this framework that represents God's sustaining presence, like a spiritual energy that keeps things from falling apart completely.
definitions.example: Like an invisible force field that prevents total chaos.

definitions.definition: The energy that exists even in empty space, according to quantum physics; it's always there, even when nothing else is.
definitions.example: Like the hum of a refrigerator that's always on, even when it's empty.

definitions.definition: An invisible field that gives particles their mass; without it, everything would be weightless and fly apart.
definitions.example: Like a thick syrup that slows down particles and makes them heavy.

definitions.definition: The lowest possible energy level a system can have; it can't go any lower.
definitions.example: A ball resting at the bottom of a valley—it can't roll any further down.

definitions.definition: God's kindness that he gives to everyone, not just believers, like sunshine and rain and the ability to live.
definitions.example: Even people who don't believe in God still enjoy good food and friendship.

definitions.definition: The study of heat, energy, and how things change from ordered to disordered.
definitions.example: Why ice melts in a warm room and why you can't unscramble an egg.

definitions.definition: How accurately information is passed from one person or generation to the next without getting distorted.
definitions.example: Like playing the telephone game—the message gets garbled the more people it passes through.

definitions.definition: When a message or signal gets weaker or more distorted as it travels or is copied.
definitions.example: A radio station that gets staticky the farther you drive from the tower.

definitions.definition: The direction in which time seems to flow, from order to disorder; why we remember the past but not the future.
definitions.example: An egg can break into a mess, but it can't unbreak itself.

definitions.definition: A number that tells you how well a mathematical model fits the data; 1 is perfect, 0 is no fit at all.
definitions.example: Like a grade on a test: 0.888 means the model explains 88.8% of what's happening.

definitions.definition: A line that a curve gets closer and closer to but never actually touches.
definitions.example: A car approaching a stop sign—it gets nearer and nearer but never quite reaches it if it keeps slowing down forever.

definitions.definition: An old-fashioned way of saying 70 years; 'score' means 20, so three score is 60, plus ten is 70.
definitions.example: If someone says 'fourscore and seven,' they mean 87 years.

definitions.definition: An old way of saying 80 years; four times 20 equals 80.
definitions.example: A person who lives to fourscore is 80 years old.

definitions.definition: The time before the great flood described in the Bible, when Noah built the ark.
definitions.example: Like the 'olden days' before a big disaster changed everything.

definitions.definition: The time after Adam and Eve disobeyed God in the Garden of Eden, when sin and death entered the world.
definitions.example: Like after a big mistake that changes everything for the worse.

definitions.definition: A founding father or leader of a family or tribe, especially in the Bible.
definitions.example: Abraham is a famous patriarch of the Jewish people.

definitions.definition: Relating to the study of how diseases and health patterns spread in populations.
definitions.example: Scientists use epidemiological data to track how many people get the flu each year.

definitions.definition: Whether something actually happened in history or is just a story.
definitions.example: Historians debate the historicity of King Arthur—was he a real person?

definitions.definition: A decrease that happens at a steady rate, like losing 10 dollars every week.
definitions.example: A straight line going downhill on a graph.

definitions.definition: Growing or shrinking very fast because each step multiplies the previous one.
definitions.example: A virus spreading where each person infects two others, who each infect two more.

definitions.definition: A starting point or reference level used for comparison.
definitions.example: Your normal heart rate at rest is your baseline; exercise makes it go up.

definitions.definition: A flat, stable period after a time of change, where things stop increasing or decreasing.
definitions.example: After losing weight quickly, your weight might hit a plateau and stay the same for a while.

definitions.definition: The specific mathematical equation that describes a relationship between variables.
definitions.example: The formula y = 2x + 1 is a functional form for a straight line.

definitions.definition: Cannot be made simpler or broken down into smaller parts.
definitions.example: A single Lego brick is irreducible—you can't take it apart further.

definitions.definition: The smallest amount of energy that exists in empty space, even at absolute zero temperature.
definitions.example: Like the faint hum of the universe that never goes away.

definitions.definition: Completely emptied of matter or energy.
definitions.example: A vacuum flask has the air evacuated to keep drinks hot or cold.

definitions.definition: A connection or interaction between two systems that affects each other.
definitions.example: Two gears locked together—when one turns, the other turns too.

definitions.definition: A detailed description of how something should be made or how it works.
definitions.example: A recipe is a specification for baking a cake.

definitions.definition: The process of passing something through an intermediate step, which can change it.
definitions.example: A game of telephone where the message changes as it's passed from person to person.

definitions.definition: Able to be passed from parent to child, like eye color or certain traits.
definitions.example: Height is heritable—tall parents tend to have tall children.

definitions.definition: The perspective of God, who exists outside of time and sees everything at once.
definitions.example: Like watching a movie from start to finish all at the same time.

definitions.definition: Replaces or overrides something older or less important.
definitions.example: A new law supersedes an old one, so you follow the new rule.
